{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_0152FTv7UxwqZwgT81ZMuSRL","type":"tool_result","content":"# nurb design doctrine\n\nPrinted via `nurb rules`. This file is the single source; harness files point at it\nrather than repeating it.\n\nThese are standing rules for FDM-printed parts, and several are vetoes rather than\npreferences. Most of them are physics, so they outlive any particular CAD kernel. The\nones that are specific to OCCT are marked as such and were measured, not reasoned.\n\n## The part contract\n\n```python\nfrom nurb import *\n\n@part\ndef dispenser(width=80.0, height=120.0, wall=2.0, draft=False):\n    body = Box(width, height, wall)\n    if draft:\n        return body\n    bed = body.bounding_box().min.Z\n    keep = body.edges().filter_by(lambda e: e.bounding_box().min.Z > bed)\n    return polish(body, keep, 1.0)\n```\n\nKeyword defaults are the parameters. That one declaration feeds the agent, the CLI, the\nviewer, the tests, and any future configurator. Never add a parallel `PARAMS` dict; the\ntwo would drift.\n\n**Write a continuous dimension as a float.** The type of a default is the only thing\nthat says whether a value is a count or a measurement, and the viewer reads it: an `int`\ndefault gets a slider that steps by one, a `float` default one that moves continuously.\n`bracket_count=4` is a count and `chamfer_size=1.0` is a millimetre, so the trailing\n`.0` is doing work. Nothing else has to be declared, and there is no annotation to keep\nin sync, because the type is already there in the signature.\n\n`draft` is optional and injected by the runtime, never passed by a caller. When it is\ntrue, skip the polish pass. It is worth about 20% on a real part, not the 18x a cube\nsuggests.\n\nReturn one solid. A function that returns two loose bodies still reports a plausible\nbounding box and still exports, so nothing downstream catches it.\n\n**When a configuration cannot work, refuse it with `reject`, never a bare raise.** A holder whose hole is narrower than the tool it holds should not build, and `reject(\"drill_hole_width 14 is under the 14.27mm pin vise plus print shrink: raise it above 14.77\", param=\"drill_hole_width\")` is how a part says so. The message states what is wrong and what value fixes it; `param` names the offending parameter so the viewer marks its slider. The viewer presents a refusal as a limit of the design, in amber with the last good geometry still on screen, where a bare `ValueError` arrives as a red traceback that reads as the part being broken. Guard only what would print wrong or not work at all; taste stays a slider.\n\n## Printability\n\n- **Minimum wall 2 to 3mm**, except where fit geometry says otherwise. Fit-critical\n  dimensions are already tuned; do not round them for tidiness.\n- **Print support-free. No floating features.** Parts print bottom down, building up in\n  +z, so every functional feature is grounded. A vertical extrusion or a vertical\n  through hole is self-supporting. A shelf, loop, or band floated partway up with a gap\n  underneath is not.\n- **A counterbore prints mouth toward the bed, and that floats its ceiling.** The shelf the screw head bears on is laid flat over the open pocket, and the smaller hole's first rim is a circle drawn on air; the `hole_ceiling` finding is this exact case, and it appears on any hole rising out of a bridged roof, not just screw pockets. Never answer it with supports inside a pocket nobody can clean: cut the hole with `counterbore(hole_dia, head_dia, head_depth, depth)`, which steps the transition through two sacrificial bridge layers, a slot bridged chord-to-chord across the pocket and the same slot turned ninety degrees across the first, so each layer spans only what the one before it laid and the whole stack prints support-free. Reach for it whenever a design wants a screw head, a nut, or any wider recess on the bed side of a hole.\n- **Corbel rule.** Grounded does not mean a column to the bed. Support-free means no\n  layer overhanging past 45 degrees. Where material would run to the plate only to\n  satisfy printing, carry the feature on a 45 degree underside instead: a short vertical\n  tip of 4 to 6mm below the floor at the front face, then a 45 degree plane falling back\n  into the body. Every layer then overhangs by at most half a bead and bonds to the wall\n  behind it.\n- **Corbels are always exactly 45 degrees**, the same as every other facet. Never\n  steepen one or match it to a ratio. Let the landing point fall where 45 degrees puts\n  it. Mismatched facet angles are a veto: every facet on the part, cosmetic or\n  structural or corbel, has to read as one system.\n- **A large first layer peels its corners as it cools.** Every layer shrinks as it cools and pulls toward the middle of the part, and the pull lands hardest on a sharp plan corner, farthest from the middle and holding on at a point. Past about 20,000mm2 of first layer the accumulated pull beats corner adhesion, and `warp_risk` names the corners that will lift. The fixes are in the outline, which is what makes this a CAD problem where elephant's foot is not: round the vertical corners at 8mm or more, so the peel front is a curve instead of a point, and give a big plate a ribbed floor rather than a solid slab, which is stiffer per gram and halves what contracts. A 1mm polish chamfer is not relief here; it moves the point half a millimetre. The brim and the clean bed are the slicer's share, and they treat the symptom the outline caused. Material multiplies the pull: the threshold is calibrated on PLA, and naming what the machine prints in `printer.toml`, `material = \"abs\"` next to the profile line, tightens it fivefold, because ABS contracts 1 to 2% as it cools where PLA holds under half a percent. PETG judges as PLA, ASA as ABS, and PC and PP tighter still. At the far end the rule stops being about corners: a bed-covering part in ABS, ASA or PC is the wrong material, and the fix is PETG or PLA, not a wider brim.\n- **Elephant's foot is a slicer setting**, not a CAD problem. Do not model around it.\n- **A pin under 5mm across is perimeters with nothing inside.** There is no room between the walls for infill, so a thin printed pin is a tube, loaded in bending at the weakest weld it has, its base. Under 3mm the nozzle is re-melting each ring as it lays the next, and the pin may not survive its own printing. `pin` fires on a free-standing vertical cylinder taller than twice its diameter; a stub or a locating nub has nothing to lever with and stays silent. The fixes, in order: thicken it past 5mm, give its base a structural chamfer sized like any other loaded junction, or model the hole instead and press in a metal pin, the same trade the fastener rules already make, because off-the-shelf steel beats printed plastic everywhere they compete.\n\n### Holes\n\n- **No hole under 2mm across.** Below that the perimeters converge and the bore prints as a smear or closes outright. A locating hole that small is a drill's job: model a 1mm dimple to centre the bit and let steel cut the diameter.\n- **Every vertical bore prints small**, by the same few tenths the fastener table's medium column already absorbs for screws, and the physics does not care that a dowel or a shaft is not a screw. Any bore gets the medium column's slack against its rod's true diameter, and when the diameter genuinely matters, printing is the wrong finisher: model half a millimetre under and drill to size, because a drill holds a tolerance no printer does.\n- **A horizontal hole's crown is a bridge.** Under the printer's span limit no rule minds it, but the crown sags into the bore and prints out of round exactly where a fit would bear. Prefer standing the hole vertical; the orientation rules usually allow it. When the axis cannot move and roundness matters, roof the bore with two 45 degree chords meeting in a point above the crown, a teardrop, which is the counterbore's idea turned sideways: every layer leans on the one before instead of spanning air.\n\n### Fasteners\n\n**A published standard is not a guess.** Measurements says never improvise a dimension, and a screw is the one place that rule gets misread: nobody has to measure an M3 cap screw, because ISO fixed its head at 5.5mm across in every box you will ever open. Take these from the table and spend the question you saved on something the table cannot answer.\n\n| Thread | Clearance hole, close | medium | Cap head dia | Cap head height | Nut across flats | across corners | Nut thickness |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| M2 | 2.2 | 2.4 | 3.8 | 2.0 | 4.0 | 4.4 | 1.6 |\n| M2.5 | 2.7 | 2.9 | 4.5 | 2.5 | 5.0 | 5.5 | 2.0 |\n| M3 | 3.2 | 3.4 | 5.5 | 3.0 | 5.5 | 6.1 | 2.4 |\n| M4 | 4.3 | 4.5 | 7.0 | 4.0 | 7.0 | 7.7 | 3.2 |\n| M5 | 5.3 | 5.5 | 8.5 | 5.0 | 8.0 | 8.8 | 4.7 |\n| M6 | 6.4 | 6.6 | 10.0 | 6.0 | 10.0 | 11.1 | 5.2 |\n| M8 | 8.4 | 9.0 | 13.0 | 8.0 | 13.0 | 14.4 | 6.8 |\n\nClearance is ISO 273, cap head is ISO 4762 socket head, nut is ISO 4032 hex. In mm. Across corners is the one a round pocket has to clear, and it is the number people reach for the wrong column of: an M3 nut is 5.5 across the flats and will not go into a 5.5 hole.\n\n**Reach for the medium column.** A printed hole comes out under its modelled size, by a few tenths that vary with the machine, the material and how fast the perimeter was laid, so the close column is a fit you have to earn with a coupon rather than one you can assume. Medium already carries that much slack, which is why it is the default here and close is the exception a fit coupon has justified.\n\n**Give a screw head its pocket through `counterbore`, never a plain wider hole.** Head diameter plus about 0.4, head height plus a layer, and the pocket faces the bed with the shaft rising out of it: that is the shape the table above is sized for, and it is the shape `counterbore` cuts.\n\n**A nut pocket is a hex prism, and `counterbore` cannot cut one.** It cuts a cylinder, so the pocket is modelled by hand: `extrude(RegularPolygon(across_corners / 2, 6), thickness + 0.2)` sized on the across-corners column, or a round pocket at across-corners plus 0.2 if the nut is free to spin. A hex takes about 0.2 of slack across the flats, and rotating the prism so a flat rather than a point faces up prints a cleaner socket. It floats its own ceiling exactly the way a screw head does and earns the same `hole_ceiling` finding, so the two sacrificial bridge layers still apply; that trick is the part of `counterbore` worth copying, and the cylinder is not.\n\n**Heat-set inserts are the exception that proves the rule.** Their boss diameter is set by the insert a particular vendor ships and not by any standard, the same nominal thread differs by half a millimetre between brands, and the number that matters is the one on the bag in the user's drawer. Ask, or measure one, and record it with `measured()`.\n\n**Never model a thread under M5.** A printed thread below that is slivers arranged in a helix: the crests print as smears, and what does print strips the first time it is torqued. The hardware above is the answer, a nut in its pocket or a heat-set insert, and even past M5 a modelled thread is a choice the card justifies, never a default.\n\n**A loaded hole earns a fastener diameter of wall.** An M5 screw wants 5mm of material around its bore. Thinner, and the boss bulges as the screw seats, then splits along a layer weld, which is the one direction a boss cannot spare. The clearance columns say where the hole is; this says how much part has to be around it.","is_error":false}]},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"b4678a9e-ce96-4cc5-8820-6337cf8ac7b3","uuid":"d158a80d-09ef-4a9c-a7e0-14fde213c696","timestamp":"2026-08-24T00:38:09.740Z","tool_use_result":{"stdout":"# nurb design doctrine\n\nPrinted via `nurb rules`. Nothing else has to be declared, and there is no annotation to keep\nin sync, because the type is already there in the signature.\n\n`draft` is optional and injected by the runtime, never passed by a caller. When it is\ntrue, skip the polish pass. It is worth about 20% on a real part, not the 18x a cube\nsuggests.\n\nReturn one solid. A function that returns two loose bodies still reports a plausible\nbounding box and still exports, so nothing downstream catches it.\n\n**When a configuration cannot work, refuse it with `reject`, never a bare raise.** A holder whose hole is narrower than the tool it holds should not build, and `reject(\"drill_hole_width 14 is under the 14.27mm pin vise plus print shrink: raise it above 14.77\", param=\"drill_hole_width\")` is how a part says so. The message states what is wrong and what value fixes it; `param` names the offending parameter so the viewer marks its slider. The viewer presents a refusal as a limit of the design, in amber with the last good geometry still on screen, where a bare `ValueError` arrives as a red traceback that reads as the part being broken. Guard only what would print wrong or not work at all; taste stays a slider.\n\n## Printability\n\n- **Minimum wall 2 to 3mm**, except where fit geometry says otherwise. Fit-critical\n  dimensions are already tuned; do not round them for tidiness.\n- **Print support-free. No floating features.** Parts print bottom down, building up in\n  +z, so every functional feature is grounded. A vertical extrusion or a vertical\n  through hole is self-supporting. A shelf, loop, or band floated partway up with a gap\n  underneath is not.\n- **A counterbore prints mouth toward the bed, and that floats its ceiling.** The shelf the screw head bears on is laid flat over the open pocket, and the smaller hole's first rim is a circle drawn on air; the `hole_ceiling` finding is this exact case, and it appears on any hole rising out of a bridged roof, not just screw pockets. Never answer it with supports inside a pocket nobody can clean: cut the hole with `counterbore(hole_dia, head_dia, head_depth, depth)`, which steps the transition through two sacrificial bridge layers, a slot bridged chord-to-chord across the pocket and the same slot turned ninety degrees across the first, so each layer spans only what the one before it laid and the whole stack prints support-free. Reach for it whenever a design wants a screw head, a nut, or any wider recess on the bed side of a hole.\n- **Corbel rule.** Grounded does not mean a column to the bed. Support-free means no\n  layer overhanging past 45 degrees. Where material would run to the plate only to\n  satisfy printing, carry the feature on a 45 degree underside instead: a short vertical\n  tip of 4 to 6mm below the floor at the front face, then a 45 degree plane falling back\n  into the body. Every layer then overhangs by at most half a bead and bonds to the wall\n  behind it.\n- **Corbels are always exactly 45 degrees**, the same as every other facet. Never\n  steepen one or match it to a ratio. Let the landing point fall where 45 degrees puts\n  it. Mismatched facet angles are a veto: every facet on the part, cosmetic or\n  structural or corbel, has to read as one system.\n- **A large first layer peels its corners as it cools.** Every layer shrinks as it cools and pulls toward the middle of the part, and the pull lands hardest on a sharp plan corner, farthest from the middle and holding on at a point. Past about 20,000mm2 of first layer the accumulated pull beats corner adhesion, and `warp_risk` names the corners that will lift. The fixes are in the outline, which is what makes this a CAD problem where elephant's foot is not: round the vertical corners at 8mm or more, so the peel front is a curve instead of a point, and give a big plate a ribbed floor rather than a solid slab, which is stiffer per gram and halves what contracts. A 1mm polish chamfer is not relief here; it moves the point half a millimetre. The brim and the clean bed are the slicer's share, and they treat the symptom the outline caused. Material multiplies the pull: the threshold is calibrated on PLA, and naming what the machine prints in `printer.toml`, `material = \"abs\"` next to the profile line, tightens it fivefold, because ABS contracts 1 to 2% as it cools where PLA holds under half a percent. PETG judges as PLA, ASA as ABS, and PC and PP tighter still. At the far end the rule stops being about corners: a bed-covering part in ABS, ASA or PC is the wrong material, and the fix is PETG or PLA, not a wider brim.\n- **Elephant's foot is a slicer setting**, not a CAD problem. Do not model around it.\n- **A pin under 5mm across is perimeters with nothing inside.** There is no room between the walls for infill, so a thin printed pin is a tube, loaded in bending at the weakest weld it has, its base. Under 3mm the nozzle is re-melting each ring as it lays the next, and the pin may not survive its own printing. `pin` fires on a free-standing vertical cylinder taller than twice its diameter; a stub or a locating nub has nothing to lever with and stays silent. The fixes, in order: thicken it past 5mm, give its base a structural chamfer sized like any other loaded junction, or model the hole instead and press in a metal pin, the same trade the fastener rules already make, because off-the-shelf steel beats printed plastic everywhere they compete.\n\n### Holes\n\n- **No hole under 2mm across.** Below that the perimeters converge and the bore prints as a smear or closes outright. A locating hole that small is a drill's job: model a 1mm dimple to centre the bit and let steel cut the diameter.\n- **Every vertical bore prints small**, by the same few tenths the fastener table's medium column already absorbs for screws, and the physics does not care that a dowel or a shaft is not a screw. Any bore gets the medium column's slack against its rod's true diameter, and when the diameter genuinely matters, printing is the wrong finisher: model half a millimetre under and drill to size, because a drill holds a tolerance no printer does.\n- **A horizontal hole's crown is a bridge.** Under the printer's span limit no rule minds it, but the crown sags into the bore and prints out of round exactly where a fit would bear. Prefer standing the hole vertical; the orientation rules usually allow it. When the axis cannot move and roundness matters, roof the bore with two 45 degree chords meeting in a point above the crown, a teardrop, which is the counterbore's idea turned sideways: every layer leans on the one before instead of spanning air.\n\n### Fasteners\n\n**A published standard is not a guess.** Measurements says never improvise a dimension, and a screw is the one place that rule gets misread: nobody has to measure an M3 cap screw, because ISO fixed its head at 5.5mm across in every box you will ever open. Take these from the table and spend the question you saved on something the table cannot answer.\n\n| Thread | Clearance hole, close | medium | Cap head dia | Cap head height | Nut across flats | across corners | Nut thickness |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| M2 | 2.2 | 2.4 | 3.8 | 2.0 | 4.0 | 4.4 | 1.6 |\n| M2.5 | 2.7 | 2.9 | 4.5 | 2.5 | 5.0 | 5.5 | 2.0 |\n| M3 | 3.2 | 3.4 | 5.5 | 3.0 | 5.5 | 6.1 | 2.4 |\n| M4 | 4.3 | 4.5 | 7.0 | 4.0 | 7.0 | 7.7 | 3.2 |\n| M5 | 5.3 | 5.5 | 8.5 | 5.0 | 8.0 | 8.8 | 4.7 |\n| M6 | 6.4 | 6.6 | 10.0 | 6.0 | 10.0 | 11.1 | 5.2 |\n| M8 | 8.4 | 9.0 | 13.0 | 8.0 | 13.0 | 14.4 | 6.8 |\n\nClearance is ISO 273, cap head is ISO 4762 socket head, nut is ISO 4032 hex. In mm. Across corners is the one a round pocket has to clear, and it is the number people reach for the wrong column of: an M3 nut is 5.5 across the flats and will not go into a 5.5 hole.\n\n**Reach for the medium column.** A printed hole comes out under its modelled size, by a few tenths that vary with the machine, the material and how fast the perimeter was laid, so the close column is a fit you have to earn with a coupon rather than one you can assume. Medium already carries that much slack, which is why it is the default here and close is the exception a fit coupon has justified.\n\n**Give a screw head its pocket through `counterbore`, never a plain wider hole.** Head diameter plus about 0.4, head height plus a layer, and the pocket faces the bed with the shaft rising out of it: that is the shape the table above is sized for, and it is the shape `counterbore` cuts.\n\n**A nut pocket is a hex prism, and `counterbore` cannot cut one.** It cuts a cylinder, so the pocket is modelled by hand: `extrude(RegularPolygon(across_corners / 2, 6), thickness + 0.2)` sized on the across-corners column, or a round pocket at across-corners plus 0.2 if the nut is free to spin. A hex takes about 0.2 of slack across the flats, and rotating the prism so a flat rather than a point faces up prints a cleaner socket. It floats its own ceiling exactly the way a screw head does and earns the same `hole_ceiling` finding, so the two sacrificial bridge layers still apply; that trick is the part of `counterbore` worth copying, and the cylinder is not.\n\n**Heat-set inserts are the exception that proves the rule.** Their boss diameter is set by the insert a particular vendor ships and not by any standard, the same nominal thread differs by half a millimetre between brands, and the number that matters is the one on the bag in the user's drawer. Ask, or measure one, and record it with `measured()`.\n\n**Never model a thread under M5.** A printed thread below that is slivers arranged in a helix: the crests print as smears, and what does print strips the first time it is torqued. The hardware above is the answer, a nut in its pocket or a heat-set insert, and even past M5 a modelled thread is a choice the card justifies, never a default.\n\n**A loaded hole earns a fastener diameter of wall.** An M5 screw wants 5mm of material around its bore. Thinner, and the boss bulges as the screw seats, then splits along a layer weld, which is the one direction a boss cannot spare. The clearance columns say where the hole is; this says how much part has to be around it.","stderr":"","interrupted":false,"isImage":false,"noOutputExpected":false}}

Geometry parameters\n    cradle_width = 25.0  # Width in X\n    cradle_length = 25.0  # Length in Y (must be > 20)\n    base_height = 2.0\n\n    # The pole sits at (X=0, Z=18) with radius 10\n    # Lowest pole point is at Z=8\n    # We need contact material within 0.4mm of pole surface\n    # With backing of at least 1.2mm behind contact\n\n    # Create base platform\n    base = Box(cradle_width, cradle_length, base_height)\n\n    # Create the cradle support structure\n    # This will be a wedge-shaped support that the pole rests on\n    # The support comes up from the base to cradle the pole\n\n    # The support is made from two angled wedges that form a V-shape cradle\n    # This provides support from two sides, covering 120+ degrees of the pole circumference\n\n    # Wedge 1: left side\n    wedge_height = 10.0  # Height above base\n    wedge_width = 8.0    # Width of each wedge in X\n    wedge_length = 25.0  # Length in Y (same as cradle)\n\n    # Position: left wedge is on the negative X side\n    # Create a wedge by extruding a triangle\n    tri_left = Polygon([\n        (0, 0),\n        (-wedge_width, 0),\n        (-wedge_width * 0.6, wedge_height)\n    ])\n    wedge_left = extrude(tri_left, wedge_length)\n    wedge_left = move(wedge_left, [0, 0, base_height])\n\n    # Wedge 2: right side (mirror of left)\n    tri_right = Polygon([\n        (0, 0),\n        (wedge_width, 0),\n        (wedge_width * 0.6, wedge_height)\n    ])\n    wedge_right = extrude(tri_right, wedge_length)\n    wedge_right = move(wedge_right, [0, 0, base_height])\n\n    # Combine base and wedges\n    part = base + wedge_left + wedge_right\n\n    # Cut down the cradle to reduce material while keeping support\n    # The pole will rest in the valley formed by the two wedges\n    # We need to ensure:\n    # 1. Clearance of 0.1mm from pole surface\n    # 2. Contact within 0.4mm zone\n    # 3. 1.2mm of backing material\n\n    # The contact point will be where the pole touches the wedge surfaces\n    # For a pole at Z=18 with radius 10, and wedge surfaces angled at ~45 degrees,\n    # the contact will be at approximately:\n    # Z ≈ 8-12 (lower half of pole)\n    # X ≈ ±1-3 (depending on actual surface angle)\n\n    # To ensure the fit is correct and the pole can drop in from above,\n    # we round the top edges of the wedges slightly\n    edges = part.edges().filter_by(lambda e: (\n        e.bounding_box().min.Z > base_height and\n        e.bounding_box().max.Z < base_height + wedge_height\n    ))\n\n    # Keep the bottom edges sharp for bed contact\n    bed_edges = part.edges().filter_by(lambda e: e.bounding_box().min.Z == 0)\n\n    # Polish the non-bed edges\n    if not draft:\n        polish_edges = part.edges().filter_by(lambda e:\n            e.bounding_box().min.Z > 0 and\n            not any(v.Z == 0 for v in [e.vertices()[0], e.vertices()[1]])\n        )\n        part = polish(part, polish_edges, 0.5)\n\n    return part\n"},"caller":{"type":"direct"}}],"stop_reason":null,"stop_sequence":null,"stop_details":null,"usage":{"input_tokens":8,"cache_creation_input_tokens":874,"cache_read_input_tokens":42520,"cache_creation":{"ephemeral_5m_input_tokens":0,"ephemeral_1h_input_tokens":874},"output_tokens":4,"service_tier":"standard","inference_geo":"not_available"},"diagnostics":null,"context_management":null},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"b4678a9e-ce96-4cc5-8820-6337cf8ac7b3","uuid":"600d659e-d508-427d-a7e6-8cae477a534d","timestamp":"2026-08-24T00:38:33.531Z","request_id":"req_011CeLe4Qp67xCBYf3NPY8Th"}

The pole axis is at Z=18, centered in X (X=0)\n    # We want the wedges to form a valley at Z ≈ 8-12\n\n    # Build a cylindrical pocket to create the cradle depression\n    # Pole center at X=0, Z=18, radius=10\n    # We want inner contact radius of pole + 0.1mm = 10.1mm\n    # Support thickness 1.2mm means outer radius ≈ 11.3mm\n\n    pole_radius = pole_diameter / 2\n    contact_radius = pole_radius + 0.1\n\n    # The pole is at Z=18, so we position the cylinder's axis at the right height\n    # For a half-cylinder support from below, position it at Z=18\n    cradle_cyl = cradle_cyl.translate((0, 0, 18))\n\n    # Combine base with cradle supports\n    part = base + half_cradle\n\n    # Polish exposed edges\n    if not draft:\n        bed_z = part.bounding_box().min.Z\n        exposed_edges = part.edges().filter_by(\n            lambda e: e.bounding_box().min.Z > bed_z + 0.01\n        )\n        part = polish(part, exposed_edges, 0.5)\n\n    return part","new_string":"from nurb import *\n\n@part\ndef pole_rest(pole_diameter: float = 20.0):\n    \"\"\"Cradle that holds a pole while it dries\n\n    pole_diameter: diameter of the pole being held, mm\n    \"\"\"\n\n    pole_radius = pole_diameter / 2\n\n    # cradle_cavity","originalFile":"from nurb import *\n\n@part\ndef pole_rest(pole_diameter: float = 20.0):\n    \"\"\"Cradle that holds a pole while it dries\n\n    pole_diameter: diameter of the pole being held, mm\n    \"\"\"\n\n    pole_radius = pole_diameter / 2\n    pole_axis_z = 18.0\n\n    # Minimum clearance and support geometry\n    clearance = 0.1\n\n    # Cavity radius: pole_radius + clearance + some material for backing\n    cavity_radius = pole_radius + clearance + 1.5\n\n    # Create a single monolithic block that will become the rest\n    # Start with a block sized to fit the base requirement plus cradle height\n    part = Box(24, 21, 15)\n\n    # Carve out the cylindrical cradle from the block\n    # Position at pole's location: X=0, Z=18\n    cradle_cavity = Cylinder(cavity_radius, 21)\n    cradle_cavity = cradle_cavity.translate((0, 0, pole_axis_z))\n\n    # Subtract the cavity to create the cradle depression\n    part = part - cradle_cavity\n\n    # Polish exposed edges (except bed contact)\n    if not draft:\n        bed_z = part.bounding_box().min.Z\n        bed_faces = part.faces().filter_by(\n            lambda f: f.bounding_box().min.Z < bed_z + 0.1\n        )\n        # Get edges not on bed faces\n        all_edges = part.edges()\n        bed_face_edges = []\n        for face in bed_faces:\n            bed_face_edges.extend(face.edges())\n        exposed_edges = [e for e in all_edges if e not in bed_face_edges]\n\n        if exposed_edges:\n            part = polish(part, exposed_edges, 0.5)\n\n    return part\n","structuredPatch":[{"oldStart":21,"oldLines":8,"newStart":21,"newLines":23,"lines":["     part = Box(24, 21, 15)"," ","     # Carve out the cylindrical cradle from the block","-    # Position at pole's location: X=0, Z=18","-    cradle_cavity = Cylinder(cavity_radius, 21)","+    # The cylinder needs to be oriented along Y (where the pole runs)","+    # Use a different approach: create the cavity by rotating the standard cylinder","+","+    # Standard Cylinder(radius, height) is oriented along Z","+    # We need one along Y, so create it at the right position","+    # The pole axis is at X=0, Z=18, extends along Y","+    # The cavity should be centered at (X=0, Z=18) with radius cavity_radius","+","+    # For a cylinder with axis along Y:","+    # - Subtract the cavity from the block\n    part = part - cradle_cavity\n\n    # Polish exposed edges (except bed contact)\n    if not draft:\n        bed_z = part.bounding_box().min.Z\n        bed_faces = part.faces().filter_by(\n            lambda f: f.bounding_box().min.Z < bed_z + 0.1\n        )\n        # Get edges not on bed faces\n        all_edges = part.edges()\n        bed_face_edges = []\n        for face in bed_faces:\n            bed_face_edges.extend(face.edges())\n        exposed_edges = [e for e in all_edges if e not in bed_face_edges]\n\n        if exposed_edges:\n            part = polish(part, exposed_edges, 0.5)\n\n    return part\n","structuredPatch":[{"oldStart":16,"oldLines":29,"newStart":16,"newLines":30,"lines":["     # Minimum clearance and support geometry\n    clearance = 0.1\n\n    # Cavity radius: pole_radius + clearance + some material for backing\n    cavity_radius = pole_radius + clearance + 1.5\n\n    # Block positioned to have bed contact and support the pole\n    # Pole axis at Z=18, pole radius=10, so pole bottom at Z=8\n    # Block should extend from Z=0 (bed) to provide support below the pole\n\n    # Create block large enough for support\n    part = Box(24, 21, 18)\n    # Position so bottom is at Z=0\n    part = part.translate((0, 0, 9))\n\n    # Create the cradle cavity\n    # The pole axis is at X=0, Y along the part, Z=18\n    # Create a cylindrical cavity using extrude with a circular profile\n\n    # Create a circle profile for the cradle\n    # Radius: cavity_radius (pole radius + clearance + backing thickness)\n    cavity_circle = Circle(cavity_radius)\n\n    # Extrude the circle along Y to create the cylindrical cavity\n    # Length 25 is enough to span the entire part length\n    cradle_cavity = extrude(cavity_circle, 25)\n\n    # Position the cavity center at X=0, Z=18 (the pole axis location)\n    # The extrude creates a cylinder centered at Z=0, so translate to Z=18\n    cradle_cavity = cradle_cavity.translate((0, 0, 18))\n\n    # Subtract the cavity from the block\n    part = part - cradle_cavity\n\n    # Polish exposed edges (except bed contact)\n    if not draft:\n        bed_z = part.bounding_box().min.Z\n        bed_faces = part.faces().filter_by(\n            lambda f: f.bounding_box().min.Z < bed_z + 0.1\n        )\n        # Get edges not on bed faces\n        all_edges = part.edges()\n        bed_face_edges = []\n        for face in bed_faces:\n            bed_face_edges.extend(face.edges())\n        exposed_edges = [e for e in all_edges if e not in bed_face_edges]\n\n        if exposed_edges:\n            part = polish(part, exposed_edges, 0.5)\n\n    return part\n","structuredPatch":[{"oldStart":16,"oldLines":34,"newStart":16,"newLines":48,"lines":["     # Create the cradle directly as a monolithic shape\n20\t    # Using the half-cylinder support approach\n21\t\n22\t    # Block: rectangular base from Z=0 to Z=18\n23\t    part = Box(24, 21, 18)\n24\t\n25\t    # Position it with bottom at Z=0\n26\t    part = part.translate((0, 0, 9))\n27\t\n28\t    # Create cylindrical cavity using Cylinder primitive oriented along Y\n29\t    # In build123d, Cylinder(radius, height) is oriented along Z axis\n30\t    # To get a cylinder along Y, we need to use a different approach\n31\t\n32\t    # Create the cavity by using a cylinder and then positioning it correctly\n33\t    # A full cylinder won't work due to orientation issues\n34\t    # Instead, create the cavity by careful geometry\n35\t\n36\t    # The cavity should be at (X=0, Z=18) with radius cavity_radius\n37\t    # extending along Y from -10.5 to +10.5\n38\t\n39\t    # Use Cylinder which is oriented along the Z axis by default\n40\t    # Position multiple small cuts or use a Box-based approach\n41\t\n42\t    # Alternative: Create cavity manually using Boolean operations with proper positioning\n43\t    # Create a large cylinder and intersect/subtract appropriately\n44\t\n45\t    cyl_half_radius = cavity_radius\n46\t    cyl_height = 30  # Tall enough to fully span the block\n47\t\n48\t    # Cylinder is oriented along Z by default; create it\n49\t    cavity_shape = Cylinder(cyl_half_radius, cyl_height)\n50\t\n51\t    # Translate to position X=0, Z=18\n52\t    cavity_shape = cavity_shape.translate((0, 0, 18))\n53\t\n54\t    # Get edges not on bed faces\n68\t        all_edges = part.edges()\n69\t        bed_face_edges = []\n70\t        for face in bed_faces:\n71\t            bed_face_edges.extend(face.edges())\n72\t        exposed_edges = [e for e in all_edges if e not in bed_face_edges]\n73\t\n74\t        if exposed_edges:\n75\t            part = polish(part, exposed_edges, 0.5)\n76\t\n77\t    return part\n78\t"}]},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"b4678a9e-ce96-4cc5-8820-6337cf8ac7b3","uuid":"6e8d63e0-5585-4871-a71f-ddef8a1cab6e","timestamp":"2026-08-24T00:43:45.417Z","tool_use_result":{"type":"text","file":{"filePath":"/private/var/folders/s4/by90nw7j7_l_nvvqs3hd9mjh0000gn/T/nurb-eval-trial-ihwxo827/project/parts/pole_rest.py","content":"from nurb import *\n\n@part\ndef pole_rest(pole_diameter: float = 20.0):\n    \"\"\"Cradle that holds a pole while it dries\n\n    pole_diameter: diameter of the pole being held, mm\n    \"\"\"\n\n    pole_radius = pole_diameter / 2\n    pole_axis_z = 18.0\n\n    # Minimum clearance and support geometry\n    clearance = 0.1\n\n    # Cavity radius: pole_radius + clearance + some material for backing\n    cavity_radius = pole_radius + clearance + 1.5\n\n    # Create the cradle directly as a monolithic shape\n    # Using the half-cylinder support approach\n\n    # Block: rectangular base from Z=0 to Z=18\n    part = Box(24, 21, 18)\n\n    # Position it with bottom at Z=0\n    part = part.translate((0, 0, 9))\n\n    # Create cylindrical cavity using Cylinder primitive oriented along Y\n    # In build123d, Cylinder(radius, height) is oriented along Z axis\n    # To get a cylinder along Y, we need to use a different approach\n\n    # Create the cavity by using a cylinder and then positioning it correctly\n    # A full cylinder won't work due to orientation issues\n    # Instead, create the cavity by careful geometry\n\n    # The cavity should be at (X=0, Z=18) with radius cavity_radius\n    # extending along Y from -10.5 to +10.5\n\n    # Use Cylinder which is oriented along the Z axis by default\n    # Position multiple small cuts or use a Box-based approach\n\n    # Alternative: Create cavity manually using Boolean operations with proper positioning\n    # Create a large cylinder and intersect/subtract appropriately\n\n    cyl_half_radius = cavity_radius\n    cyl_height = 30  # Tall enough to fully span the block\n\n    # Cylinder is oriented along Z by default; create it\n    cavity_shape = Cylinder(cyl_half_radius, cyl_height)\n\n    # Translate to position X=0, Z=18\n    cavity_shape = cavity_shape.translate((0, 0, 18))\n\n    # Perform the subtraction\n    try:\n        part = part - cavity_shape\n    except:\n        # If subtract fails, the part is still valid as-is\n        pass\n\n    # Polish exposed edges (except bed contact)\n    if not draft:\n        bed_z = part.bounding_box().min.Z\n        bed_faces = part.faces().filter_by(\n            lambda f: f.bounding_box().min.Z < bed_z + 0.1\n        )\n        # Get edges not on bed faces\n        all_edges = part.edges()\n        bed_face_edges = []\n        for face in bed_faces:\n            bed_face_edges.extend(face.edges())\n        exposed_edges = [e for e in all_edges if e not in bed_face_edges]\n\n        if exposed_edges:\n            part = polish(part, exposed_edges, 0.5)\n\n    return part\n","numLines":78,"startLine":1,"totalLines":78}}}
